title: Experimentally Testable Quantum Advantage in Shallow Circuits
abstract: Experimental tests of shallow-circuit quantum advantage require explicit classical bounds at finite circuit sizes. We refine the finite-size classical soundness bound of Aasnaess's graph-distributed construction to depend linearly on the number of players. Combined with standard disjoint-player repetition, this gives a two-round test on a single processor for any finite nonlocal game with a finite-dimensional perfect quantum strategy and classical winning probability $γ<1$, with arbitrarily small classical success. The method is based on playing $m$ copies with disjoint players and teleporting each player's register to a uniformly random one of $N$ sites before the questions are revealed. Each answer bit of a depth-$D$, fan-in-$K$ classical response with fixed wiring depends on at most $K^D$ question wires, making cross-player dependencies unlikely when $N$ is large. The quantum implementation has constant depth per round and wins with certainty. A classical device wins with probability at most $γ^m+O(mK^D/N)$, which vanishes as $O(\log N/N)$ for $m=\lceil\log_{1/γ}N\rceil$ at fixed $D$ and $K$. We present an explicit proposal for an experimentally testable quantum advantage with 99 qubits.
summary: This work establishes a rigorous, experimentally testable method to prove quantum advantage in shallow quantum circuits by analyzing nonlocal games. It refines classical bounds to show that the classical success probability vanishes rapidly ($O(\log N/N)$) as the number of sites $N$ increases. This provides a clear roadmap for near-term quantum hardware demonstrations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of experimentally demonstrating quantum advantage using shallow quantum circuits by refining the classical bounds for nonlocal games.
main_result: They provide an explicit, experimentally testable protocol showing that the classical winning probability decays as $O(\log N/N)$ for large host graphs, while the quantum device wins with certainty.
method: The method involves a two-round protocol using quantum teleportation across a host graph of $N$ sites, combined with disjoint-player repetition to suppress classical correlations.
model_or_system: The model is based on testing nonlocal games ($G$) using $m$ disjoint copies played on a host graph of $N$ sites. The quantum advantage is demonstrated by comparing the quantum winning probability (unity) against the derived classical bound.
key_observables: Classical winning probability ($p_c$), quantum winning probability ($\omega_q$), and the required number of copies ($m$).
important_parameters: The depth ($D$) and fan-in ($K$) of the classical response circuit, and the number of sites ($N$) in the host graph.
main_assumptions: The classical competitor is modeled as a randomized circuit with limited online depth ($D$) and fan-in ($K$), and the quantum implementation is assumed to be ideal (noiseless) for the theoretical bound.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two-round protocol involving teleportation and measurement, and tables list classical thresholds ($B_c$) for various circuit depths ($D$) and qubit numbers ($Q$).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by refining the classical soundness bound, details the two-round protocol, derives the vanishing classical bound $O(\log N/N)$, and concludes with an explicit proposal for a 99-qubit test.
why_interesting: It provides concrete, resource-aware protocols for quantum advantage testing, which is crucial for bridging theoretical quantum complexity with near-term experimental hardware capabilities.
